Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

info.title: Why Computational Cognitive Science? Specifying Social Science Theories as Cognitive Agents
keywords: media effects Why Computational Cognitive Science? Specifying Social Science Theories as Cognitive Agents

author.affiliation:
Department of Journalism and Public Relations
								Jeju National University
								
									Jeju
									Republic of Korea

text.text: Social science theories about how people and environments change each other are mostly stated in words.
Verbal statements leave open the quantities and functional forms needed to derive outcomes.
Tests of association cannot distinguish the individual rules that could have produced an association, and causal structures established separately are rarely combined.

Computational cognitive science offers a remedy: it specifies theories as rules that generate individual judgment and choice, runs the rules, and checks before data collection whether rival rules can be distinguished.
Cognitive agent modeling adapts this practice to theories of person-environment relations.
Four causal structures recur in social science: the environment changes people, people select their environments, the two change each other over time, and environmental effects differ across people.
Cognitive agent modeling specifies these structures as four components of one agent: learning, choice, feedback, and individual differences.
The article compares the approach with other computational approaches and works through media effects theories as a case, giving an example specification and four propositions.

In a simulation, three rival explanations of crime viewing and fear yielded positive mean correlations, and a design alternating assigned and freely chosen exposure identified the generating specification in 96% to 100% of data sets.
media effects model holds that the size of an effect differs across people (Valkenburg & Peter, 2013).
text.formatted: media effects model holds that the size of an effect differs across people <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Valkenburg & Peter, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Together the four theories describe four causal structures: the environment changes people (environment → person), people select their environments (person → environment), the two change each other over time (transaction), and the environment's effect differs across people (moderation).
Each structure also appears in developmental, organizational, or network research, as the third section shows.

In the literatures examined below, social science theories have mostly been tested by estimating the direction and size of associations between variables, and few studies of personenvironment relations have compared the individual rules that could produce an association.
An individual rule is a stated procedure that takes what a person has seen and what the person wants and returns a judgment or a choice.
For example, a person estimates how common crime is from how easily instances of crime come to mind (Shrum, 1995).
text.formatted: For example, a person estimates how common crime is from how easily instances of crime come to mind <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Shrum, 1995)</ref>.

text.text: Rival rules are different procedures that could produce the same observed association; the fifth section compares two such rules for cultivation.

Causal inference states the assumptions under which a causal effect can be identified from observed data (Hernán & Robins, 2020), but identifying an effect does not reveal which rules produced the association.
text.formatted: Causal inference states the assumptions under which a causal effect can be identified from observed data <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Hernán & Robins, 2020)</ref>, but identifying an effect does not reveal which rules produced the association.

text.text: To ask which rules produced an association, researchers first need a theory that can be run.
Making a theory runnable takes two steps: specification and implementation.

A specification is a formal or formalizable description of the system a theory implies (see Box 1); it constrains the possible models so that a model can be re-implemented from it (Guest & Martin, 2021).
text.formatted: A specification is a formal or formalizable description of the system a theory implies (see Box 1); it constrains the possible models so that a model can be re-implemented from it <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Guest & Martin, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: One verbal statement admits several specifications, so a verbal statement alone does not determine what a theory predicts (Smaldino, 2017).
text.formatted: One verbal statement admits several specifications, so a verbal statement alone does not determine what a theory predicts <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Smaldino, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Implementation turns one specification into rules a computer can execute.
Researchers can then run the model, inspect its outputs, and compare rival models.
This article calls specification and implementation together formalization.
Computational cognitive science has long specified and formalized the rules behind human judgment and choice.
Cognitive agent modeling, as this article uses the term, adapts that practice to social science theories of person-environment relations.

The next section derives three requirements for stating theories and compares computational approaches; the third shows three limits of verbal theory; the fourth defines cognitive agent modeling; the fifth presents four types of simulation; and the sixth discusses contributions and limitations.
An agent produces behavior in a closed loop: it senses, chooses, and acts, and the consequences of its action change what it senses next (Franklin & Graesser, 1997).
text.formatted: An agent produces behavior in a closed loop: it senses, chooses, and acts, and the consequences of its action change what it senses next <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Franklin & Graesser, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: The closed loop alone does not distinguish a simple copying rule from a person deliberating.
Agents differ in what they pursue and how they choose.
An agent's description specifies its environment, sensing capabilities, actions, motivations, and action-selection architecture, or how it picks one available action (Franklin & Graesser, 1997).
text.formatted: An agent's description specifies its environment, sensing capabilities, actions, motivations, and action-selection architecture, or how it picks one available action <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Franklin & Graesser, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: Motivations and action selection answer why the agent acts as it does, so their content must come from theory.
If theory does not supply them, researchers fill them in for convenience, and the outputs then reflect the researcher's choices as much as the theory.
In what follows, an agent is a computational model of a person, and the person it models is called a participant.
For theory to supply motivations and action selection, it must state them precisely enough for a model to run, and most social science theories do not.
In social psychology, theory building has been dominated by variable-based models, which link variables without representing how agents interact (Smith & Conrey, 2007).

Requirement 2 is met by fitting rival models to repeated choices and checking recovery.

text.text: A panel survey with a few waves gives each participant only a few trials.
Two checks decide whether that is enough.

Parameter recovery simulates data from known parameter values, fits the model to those data, and asks how closely the generating values come back; if they do not, the planned study cannot interpret the estimates.

Model recovery simulates data from each of several rival models and asks whether model comparison picks the model that generated each data set; if it does not, the planned study cannot rank those models (Wilson & Collins, 2019).
text.formatted: Model recovery simulates data from each of several rival models and asks whether model comparison picks the model that generated each data set; if it does not, the planned study cannot rank those models <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Wilson & Collins, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Both checks need only simulated data, so they can be run before data collection; their conclusions hold only for the candidates, measurement conditions, and parameter ranges examined.
Requirement 3 can be met by a generative model: a model that states step by step and with probabilities how judgments and actions are produced from what an agent perceives and wants.
The term is statistical and unrelated to generative artificial intelligence.
Because each step is an explicit rule, several processes can be written as steps of one model and run together (Kleiman-Weiner et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Because each step is an explicit rule, several processes can be written as steps of one model and run together <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Kleiman-Weiner et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: In such a model, the theory states the goals from which every choice follows, so the combined processes operate as one person's rules.
Such models have rarely been used to combine the structures of person-environment theories.
Computational approaches differ in how far they specify individual rules.
A path in a structural equation model states which variable affects which, but not the rules of judgment and choice that produce it, and different rules can produce the same covariance structure.

The empirical models of computational social science estimate causal effects or predict outcomes (Hofman et al., 2021), and neither task requires stating the individual rules that produce the relations between variables.

Theory-driven approaches specify individual rules in agents, some more fully than others.
This article calls an agent thin when its rules are given as fixed numbers or simple conditions rather than computed from goals.

text.text: With an established theory for each structure, media effects research is a convenient case for examining how the theories have been stated and tested, and what remains uncombined when they are stated separately.
Three limits correspond to the three requirements.
The theories leave open the quantities and forms needed to derive outcomes (the limit of statement).
Repeatedly observed associations between environment and person cannot distinguish the individual rules that produced them (the limit of testing).
The theories themselves called for combining the structures, but in the work reviewed here no specification joined them (the limit of combination).

First, where did an observed association come from?
Research design addresses this question.

text.text: Among the formalizations reviewed here, however, none combined the four causal structures of media effects theories within one thick agent with person-specific parameters.

Definition and Agent Thickness Computational cognitive science runs agents specified from theory and tests them against empirical data; cognitive agent modeling adapts that practice to social science theories of person -environment relations.
The agent realizes a specification as a complete set of rules, each a single computation; a component groups the rules or parameters that implement one causal structure.
The approach has three features.

First, the agent chooses by planning: it computes the value of each option as how well the option is expected to achieve the goals a theory specifies, weighed against the option's cost (Baker et al., 2009).
text.formatted: First, the agent chooses by planning: it computes the value of each option as how well the option is expected to achieve the goals a theory specifies, weighed against the option's cost <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Baker et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Second, each participant has their own parameter values, estimated separately or hierarchically.

Third, the approach asks whether the specified agent generates the observed data and whether rival specifications, which differ from it in one or more rules or components, are distinguishable in those data.
It does not restrict the number of agents; interacting agents' actions change the environment the others observe (Figure 1).

text.text: Consider one participant over a series of evenings.

Each evening the participant sees some crime on television and some in daily life, revises an estimate of how common crime is, and picks the next program; under self-selected supply, what the participant picks changes what is offered the next evening.

In this loop, the four causal structures correspond to four components (Table 2): learning (revising the estimate), choice (picking a program), feedback (the carryover from one evening to the next), and individual differences (the person-specific settings that make one participant differ from another).

text.text: In this notation, each evening is a trial, and the environment is in some state, here defined by what the media offer and what the participant directly experiences.
The agent holds a belief state: its current estimate of social reality and its attitudes.
 Choice.
From the belief state, the agent computes the value Q of each available action, and a choice rule, called the policy π in decision theory, picks one.
 Learning.
After acting, the agent receives an observation of the state through an observation function O. This function gives the probability of each observation given the state and the chosen action.
The agent then updates its belief state using the state estimator SE.
 Feedback.
The chosen action changes the next state of the environment through the transition function T, and beliefs carry over to the next trial.
 Individual differences.
Person-specific parameters θᵢ enter these rules.

In the original framework, SE and Q are fixed by what an optimal agent would compute; cognitive agent modeling replaces them with the rules a theory states, so the agent can depart from optimality in the ways the theory says people do.

Box 1 specifies one agent that combines cultivation learning and selective exposure.
Its functional forms are chosen for concreteness; no parameter values are fitted to data.
An Example Specification  Actions: the programs available on trial t (in Table 3, also going out).
text.formatted: An Example Specification  Actions: the programs available on trial t (in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">3</ref>, also going out).

text.text:  Belief state (current views): bₜ holds the participant's attitude, fixed in this example, and the participant's estimate of the share of crime among events in the world.
The estimate's uncertainty is the variance of a beta distribution.
Its mean is the estimate, and its parameters sum to the number of instances observed so far.
Accuracy motivation reduces this uncertainty.
 Observation function (what is seen): oₜ = O(sₜ, aₜ) gives the crime and non-crime instances in the program chosen on trial t and in daily life, observed without error.

 State estimator (belief update; weighted average): the crime estimate is updated as wₜ•mₜ + (1 -wₜ)•d, where mₜ is the share of crime among televised instances seen so far, d is the share among directly experienced instances so far, and wₜ = hₜ / (hₜ + κᵢ) grows with the number of televised instances hₜ.

Before any television (hₜ = 0), the estimate equals d, so the measured d sets the prior estimate in b₀. κᵢ is the number of televised instances at which television and direct experience count equally; the larger κᵢ, the more slowly a participant's estimate follows television.

 Rival state estimator: replaces the weighted average with a sigmoid (S-shaped) function of the number of crime instances, televised and direct, that the participant retrieves from memory; the function is centered at a person-specific number cᵢ.
 Action value (program worth): Qₜ(a) = ωᵢ•C(a, bₜ) + (1 -ωᵢ)•U(a, bₜ), where the defense weight ωᵢ sets how much C counts.

C = 1 -|g(a) -attitude| is the consistency of program a's slant g(a) with the attitude in bₜ (defense motivation), and U is how much adding a's instances would reduce the estimate's variance, evaluated at the current estimate (accuracy motivation).
Values look one trial ahead, and costs of action are omitted.
In this example, the crime estimate reaches choice only through U, which does not differ across programs carrying equal numbers of instances.
Table 3's choice specifications add the estimate to Q, and Proposition 3 assumes that beliefs raise the value of congruent content.
 Policy (choice rule): P(aₜ = a) = exp(Qₜ(a)/τᵢ) / Σₐ′ exp(Qₜ(a′)/τᵢ).
This softmax rule has the functional form of the conditional logit model in discrete-choice analysis; a higher temperature τᵢ makes choices less sensitive to differences in program value.
 Transition function (next offer): sₜ₊₁ = T(sₜ, aₜ).

Under broadcast supply, T ignores aₜ, and a crime program is offered with probability p₀; under self-selected supply, the next trial's probability is (1 -λ)p₀ + λ after a crime program is chosen and (1 -λ)p₀ otherwise, so λ sets how strongly choices shape supply.
 Person-specific parameters: θᵢ = (κᵢ, ωᵢ, τᵢ), with cᵢ in place of κᵢ in the sigmoid specification.
The goal weights ωᵢ and 1 -ωᵢ sum to 1, which fixes the scale of Q, so ωᵢ and τᵢ can be identified separately when C and U vary independently across programs.

text.text: Cultivation theory does not specify the function by which the state estimator combines televised and directly experienced instances.

Box 1 gives two candidates, which differ in their inputs (shares versus counts of instances) as well as in shape: a weighted average that gives television more weight the more a participant watches, and a sigmoid function in which estimates rise steeply once retrieved instances exceed a certain number.

An illustrative calculation (Supplementary Material S1) ran both candidates for four kinds of viewers, crossing light versus heavy viewing with direct experience of crime that differs from or resembles television content.
Under the weighted average, the estimates of the two heavy-viewer groups converged (mainstreaming), but viewing raised estimates less among those whose experience resembled television (no resonance).
Both results hold for any values shared by the two direct-experience groups, including κ and the televised content.

For groups with direct-experience shares d₁ and d₂, the gap between their estimates is (1 -w)|d₁ -d₂|, which shrinks as television's weight w grows; the size of the viewing effect is proportional to the television-experience gap |m -d|, which is smaller when experience resembles television.
Under the sigmoid function with the S1 values, the pattern reversed: mainstreaming did not appear, and resonance did.

With more directly experienced events (18 rather than 10), heavy viewing pushed those whose experience resembled television onto the flat upper part of the curve, and resonance disappeared; with heavier exposure or a lower center, the sigmoid yielded mainstreaming without resonance.
Of the two candidates, only the sigmoid can produce resonance.
Supplementary Material S2 (seed 73) checks, before data collection, whether the two functions can be told apart.
Simulated participants shared one function and reported a crime estimate after each assigned program; all other constants stayed at their generating values.
Under these conditions, model comparison selected the generating function for nearly every data set, except with 10 trials and very noisy reports (61% for the weighted average).

Classifying each participant separately, as needed if functions differ across people, required more data: with 20 trials and moderately noisy reports, the generating function was recovered for 86% of weightedaverage and 97% of sigmoid participants, and with 10 trials as few as 54%.
Proposition 1.
Suppose televised and direct instances combine as a weighted average, and κ (how slowly estimates follow television), televised content, and viewing amounts are common to the experience groups.
Then resonance cannot occur at any parameter values.
Robust resonance in data that measure viewing and direct experience for the same participants would therefore rule out the weighted average unless κ varies with direct experience.
Mainstreaming without resonance fits both specifications.

In Box 1, the defense weight ωᵢ is fixed for each participant.

Two specifications instead let it change across trials, separating conditions that Slater (2015) states together: identity threat sets the weight in a threat specification, and the degree to which attitudes have been maintained sets it in a satisfaction specification.
When the weight falls, attitude-consistent choice weakens and the spiral can stop.
Both specifications allow this, so conditions under which their predictions diverge must be found and tested with repeated measurement.
The differential susceptibility model proposes a candidate mechanism: one susceptibility acts in two rules.
Model comparison between nested specifications can test one strict version of this dual role, in which one latent susceptibility links the two rules.

Choice susceptibility is the person-specific parameter through which a trait enters the choice rule (in Box 1, the defense weight ωᵢ), and learning susceptibility is the one through which it enters the learning rule (in Box 1, κᵢ).
In a shared-susceptibility specification, one latent susceptibility per participant determines both parameters on transformed scales (for example, logit ωᵢ and log κᵢ).
Each transformed parameter is a linear function of that susceptibility.
A separate-susceptibility specification estimates the two parameters separately; the group-level correlation between them is estimated on the same transformed scales.
Proposition 4.
Suppose the separate-susceptibility specification is fitted to all participants at once, with each participant's two susceptibilities varying around group means (a hierarchical fit).

If one latent susceptibility drives both rules, the group-level correlation between the choice and learning susceptibilities on the transformed scales should be near 1 in absolute value, and the shared-susceptibility specification should fit nearly as well as the separate one.
Parameter recovery checks whether this correlation can be estimated with the planned number of trials.

text.text: This article maps the four causal structures of person-environment theories onto four components of one thick agent.

The mapping makes four contrasts testable: rival combining functions of cultivation (Proposition 1); specifications of the four models of viewing and fear of crime, distinguished before data collection by a simulation-tested design (Proposition 2); one person's learning and choice rules under broadcast versus self-selected supply (Proposition 3); and nested specifications of susceptibility's dual role (Proposition 4).
This article also gives a criterion for specifying a generative artificial intelligence system as part of the environment or as a second agent.
Code generation lowers the cost of a first implementation, so more models are built.
Recovery checks therefore become more important for distinguishing models that test a theory from models that merely produce plausible results.

Three requirements follow.
A theory must fix the quantities (the parameters and variables a model needs) and the functional forms that combine them (Requirement 1).
Researchers must ask whether rival rules can be distinguished in data (Requirement 2).

Theories of personenvironment relations add a third: the causal structures linking person and environment must be combined in one specification, so that what happens when the environment changes can be derived from that specification (Requirement 3).
One such change is a shift from broadcast media supply to self-selected supply, in which what a person chooses shapes what the person is offered next.
The requirements build on each other.
An agent runs only once its quantities are fixed.
Before data collection, running agents shows whether rival rules are distinguishable and what one agent combining the structures yields when the environment changes.

Figure 2 Two Routes of Theory Statement and the Three Limits , crime perceptions and orientation toward alternative news reinforced each other, but crime perceptions and use of traditional news did not.

The authors offered two explanations: alternative news users may form a closed communication system in which positive feedback is pronounced, while traditional news users have reached a stable state; or the two kinds of use were measured differently.
In the agent, traditional news is modeled as a transition function that gives everyone the same content regardless of choice.
Alternative news is modeled as self-selected supply, on the assumption that choosing an alternative outlet changes what the user is offered next.
The authors did not propose this supply-based account of the stable-state explanation.

Under broadcast supply, choices change what a person sees but not what is offered next, so one loop remains (beliefs → choice → exposure → beliefs); use settles into a stable state if that loop does not amplify itself.
Under self-selected supply, choices also change supply, and this second loop can amplify itself.
Proposition 3.

If the stable-state explanation holds, panel data in which both kinds of news use are measured the same way should still show reinforcement between use and crime perceptions for alternative news but not for traditional news.
If the measurement explanation holds, the difference should disappear once measurement is equalized.
The stable-state and measurement explanations can also hold together.

Under the agent account, if beliefs raise the value of congruent content, reinforcement should grow with λ (how strongly choices shape supply), and λ would be larger where offers follow past choices, as in algorithmically curated feeds.
